# Demand Letter — Copyright Infringement

## When to use this

Use this when a party has copied, distributed, publicly displayed, publicly
performed, or made a derivative of a work the Kingdom owns, and either the
informal approach has failed or the infringement is plainly commercial. This is
rung four of the escalation ladder in `02-IP-ENFORCEMENT-PLAYBOOK`.

Send it *after* rung two, not instead of it. A short courteous message from a
named officer resolves most infringement within a day, and a formal demand sent to
someone who would have complied on request buys nothing but resentment. Send it
*instead of* a DMCA notice where the infringement is not hosted by a third-party
service, where the Kingdom wants something a takedown cannot give — an
undertaking, an accounting, a licence, attribution — or where the infringer is
identifiable and solvent.

Do not send it to a critic, a journalist, a scholar, or a parodist. Read section 7
of the playbook before deciding; enforcement against commentary converts a small
piece of criticism into a large story about an institution suppressing criticism.

## Before you send

- [ ] **Ownership is documented, not assumed.** Named author, named owner, and the
      signed writing under 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) where the author was not the Kingdom.
      Recorded in the Register of Rights with the instrument attached.
- [ ] **The registration certificate is in hand,** with its effective date of
      registration, and the § 412 position is known — whether statutory damages and
      attorney's fees are available on these facts or whether the Kingdom is
      limited to actual damages and the infringer's profits. This determines what
      the letter may say about remedies and, in practice, whether the letter is
      worth sending at all.
- [ ] **Fair use has been considered in writing** under 17 U.S.C. § 107, and the
      four-factor analysis is in the matter record. So has whether what was taken
      is protectable expression at all: names, titles, and short phrases are not
      (37 C.F.R. § 202.1(a)), and neither are ideas, systems, methods, or facts
      (17 U.S.C. § 102(b)).
- [ ] **The infringement is captured and in the Evidence Vault** with its custody
      record, per `05-EVIDENCE-AND-CHAIN-OF-CUSTODY` § 2. Capture before you
      contact. Everything vanishes within hours of this letter arriving.
- [ ] **The recipient is correctly identified** — the legal entity, not the trade
      name; the registered agent where one exists; the individual where the
      business is unincorporated. A letter to the wrong entity is answered by
      nobody.
- [ ] **A chronology exists** giving the date of creation, first publication,
      registration, first observed infringement, and every contact to date.
- [ ] **The Kingdom knows what outcome it will accept** and has authority to accept
      it. Removal? An undertaking not to repeat? Attribution? A paid licence going
      forward? Decide before drafting; the demand paragraph is the letter.
- [ ] **The deadline is one the Kingdom will actually act on,** and the follow-up
      is already in the calendar.
- [ ] **The Kingdom's own legal hold has issued.** Sending this letter fixes the
      Kingdom's preservation duty as surely as the recipient's
      (`05-EVIDENCE-AND-CHAIN-OF-CUSTODY` § 7).
- [ ] **The matter is open in the Enforcement Docket,** and the officer signing has
      authority to sign.

## The letter

```
[APEX KINGDOM LETTERHEAD — name, postal address, telephone, email]

[DATE]

VIA CERTIFIED MAIL, RETURN RECEIPT REQUESTED, AND BY EMAIL TO [ADDRESS]

[RECIPIENT LEGAL NAME]
[ATTN: NAMED INDIVIDUAL OR REGISTERED AGENT]
[STREET ADDRESS]
[CITY, STATE, ZIP]

Re:  Unauthorized use of copyrighted work — [TITLE OF WORK]
     U.S. Copyright Registration No. [NUMBER]
     Our reference: [MATTER REFERENCE]

Dear [MR./MS./MX. SURNAME]:

I write on behalf of Apex Kingdom ("the Kingdom") concerning your use of a
copyrighted work owned by the Kingdom. I ask that you read this letter
carefully and respond by [DEADLINE DATE].

THE WORK AND THE KINGDOM'S OWNERSHIP

The Kingdom owns [TITLE OF WORK], a [TYPE OF WORK] authored by [AUTHOR] and
first published on [DATE]. The work is registered with the United States
Copyright Office as Registration No. [NUMBER], with an effective date of
registration of [DATE]. A copy of the certificate of registration is
enclosed as Exhibit A. [WHERE THE AUTHOR WAS NOT THE KINGDOM: The Kingdom
holds all right, title, and interest in the work by written assignment
dated [DATE], a copy of which is enclosed as Exhibit B.]

THE USE COMPLAINED OF

[STATE WHAT WAS DONE, WITH DATES AND PARTICULARITY. FOR EXAMPLE:]

On [DATE] the Kingdom observed that the page at [URL] reproduces
[DESCRIBE PRECISELY WHAT WAS TAKEN — e.g., "pages 4 through 11 of the work
verbatim, comprising approximately 3,200 words, under the heading 'Our
Founding Principles'"]. The material appeared without attribution and
without any license from the Kingdom. It remained available as of [DATE].
Dated captures of the material are enclosed as Exhibit C.

[ADD FURTHER INSTANCES IN THE SAME FORM, EACH WITH ITS OWN DATE, LOCATION,
AND DESCRIPTION OF WHAT WAS TAKEN.]

[WHERE APPLICABLE: The material is used in connection with [DESCRIBE THE
COMMERCIAL CONTEXT — e.g., "a paid course offered at $249 per enrollment"].]

WHY THIS INFRINGES

Section 106 of the Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. § 106, gives the owner of a
copyright the exclusive rights to reproduce the work, to prepare derivative
works, to distribute copies, and to display and perform the work publicly.
The use described above exercises [SPECIFY WHICH: the reproduction,
distribution, and public display rights] without the Kingdom's
authorization. The Kingdom has granted you no license, and none of the
statutory limitations on those rights, including fair use under 17 U.S.C.
§ 107, applies to a [VERBATIM AND SUBSTANTIALLY COMPLETE / COMMERCIAL AND
NON-TRANSFORMATIVE] reproduction of this kind.

WHAT THE KINGDOM ASKS YOU TO DO

By [DEADLINE DATE], please:

1. Remove the material identified above from [URL] and from every other
   location under your control, including any cached, archived, printed, or
   redistributed copy;

2. Cease all further reproduction, distribution, public display, public
   performance, and preparation of derivative works from the work;

3. Confirm in writing that you have done so, and identify every location
   where the material was published and every party to whom it was
   distributed;

4. [WHERE THE KINGDOM WILL ACCEPT IT: Confirm in writing that you will not
   use the work again without the Kingdom's written permission];

5. [WHERE THE USE WAS COMMERCIAL AND THE KINGDOM INTENDS TO PURSUE IT:
   Provide an accounting of all revenue received in connection with the
   material identified above, together with the supporting records]; and

6. Preserve all documents and electronically stored information relating to
   your acquisition and use of the work, including correspondence, drafts,
   files, server logs, sales records, and analytics data. This letter places
   you on notice that a dispute is reasonably anticipated, and your
   obligation to preserve such material has now attached.

[WHERE THE KINGDOM IS WILLING TO LICENSE: The Kingdom would also consider a
written license permitting your continued use on reasonable terms. If that
interests you, say so in your reply and the Kingdom will send proposed
terms.]

RESPONSE

Please direct your response to me at the address or email above by
[DEADLINE DATE]. If you are represented, please have your attorney contact
me directly and I will correspond with them from that point.

The Kingdom would prefer to resolve this in correspondence, and in the
Kingdom's experience most matters of this kind are resolved that way. If
this matter is not resolved by the date above, the Kingdom will consider the
remedies available to it under the Copyright Act.

This letter is not a complete statement of the facts or of the Kingdom's
position, and nothing in it waives or limits any right, claim, or remedy
available to the Kingdom, all of which are expressly reserved.

Sincerely,

______________________________
[FULL NAME]
[OFFICE HELD], Apex Kingdom
[ADDRESS] · [TELEPHONE] · [EMAIL]

[WHERE THE SIGNING OFFICER IS NOT AN ATTORNEY: I am an officer of Apex
Kingdom and am not an attorney. This letter is sent by the Kingdom in its
own behalf as the owner of the work described above.]

Enclosures:  Exhibit A — Certificate of Registration No. [NUMBER]
             Exhibit B — [ASSIGNMENT DATED [DATE]]
             Exhibit C — Dated captures of the material at [URL]
```

## Notes

**What the letter is, in register.** Correspondence from a property owner to a
person using their property. Every choice below follows from that. It bears no
seal implying judicial authority, is captioned "Dear —" rather than as a matter in
a forum, asks rather than orders, and gives a date by which the Kingdom would like
an answer rather than a date on which something is deemed to have happened. It is
not a summons, a notice of default operating as a judgment, a lien, or an order,
and it must never be made to resemble one. That line is set out in
`01-LEGAL-POSTURE` § 4 and it does not move.

**Write it for opposing counsel reading it aloud to a judge.** That is the
audience the drafting should assume, and a letter written for it also works on the
recipient. Overstatement that reads as forceful today reads as impeachment
material in eighteen months.

### What was deliberately left out

**No threat of criminal prosecution.** Criminal copyright infringement exists
(17 U.S.C. § 506; 18 U.S.C. § 2319), and it is not the Kingdom's to threaten.
Connecticut's Rules of Professional Conduct forbid a lawyer from presenting or
threatening to present criminal charges solely to obtain an advantage in a civil
matter (Rule 4.5), and the exposure for a lay officer is worse, not better: a
demand for money backed by a threat to report a crime is the fact pattern of
extortion. Referral of a genuine crime to a prosecutor is a separate decision,
made for its own reasons, never mentioned in a letter seeking money.

**No damages figure.** The template does not say "$150,000 per work" and no draft
should. Statutory damages under 17 U.S.C. § 504(c) are available only where § 412
allows them, are awarded in the court's discretion within a range, and the maximum
requires proof of wilfulness. A number in a demand letter is a number the Kingdom
will be held to — too high and it evidences bad faith and invites a declaratory
judgment action; too low and it caps the negotiation. Cite the exclusive rights,
say the Kingdom will consider its remedies, and let the recipient's own counsel
explain the range to them. That conversation is more persuasive than anything the
Kingdom could write.

**No deadline the Kingdom will not enforce.** Fourteen or twenty-one days is
standard and sufficient. A deadline that passes without consequence teaches the
recipient, correctly, that nothing follows, and every subsequent letter from the
Kingdom is worth less. If the Kingdom is not prepared to escalate, set a deadline
anyway and escalate to the *next* available rung — a platform complaint, a
follow-up letter, a Copyright Claims Board proceeding — rather than to nothing.

**No claim of tribal jurisdiction, sovereign authority, or immunity, and no
assertion that the recipient is subject to the Kingdom's law.** The Kingdom's
position in this letter rests entirely on a federal statute that binds the
recipient whether or not they have ever heard of the Kingdom. That is the strength
of the claim, and mixing it with assertions a court will not accept is the fastest
way to make a strong letter look unserious. The letterhead says Apex Kingdom; the
signature block says the office held; nothing implies government authority or law
enforcement, and nothing implies the signer is an attorney where they are not
(Conn. Gen. Stat. § 51-88).

**No accusation of wilfulness in the first letter.** Wilfulness is worth a great
deal at judgment and nothing in correspondence, and alleging it before the
recipient has had a chance to respond forecloses the innocent explanation that
resolves most matters. The letter itself supplies notice; conduct *after* this
letter is what builds a wilfulness record.

**No demand the Kingdom would refuse if accepted.** Every numbered item is
something the Kingdom actually wants and will take. Demanding capitulation retains
a lawyer for the other side and converts a two-week matter into a two-year one.

### Two things deliberately left in

**The preservation paragraph.** Item six is doing real work: it fixes the moment
the recipient's duty to preserve attached, which is what makes a later spoliation
argument available under Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(e). It costs a sentence. Note that it
fixes the Kingdom's duty at the same moment — issue the internal hold before the
letter goes out, not after.

**The invitation to licence.** Where the Kingdom would accept a licence, saying so
converts an adversary into a customer and closes matters at a rate nothing else
approaches. Omit the paragraph where the Kingdom would not licence at any price.

### One consequence to weigh before sending

A sufficiently pointed demand letter can create a live controversy allowing the
recipient to file a declaratory judgment action — asking a court to declare there
is no infringement — in *their* home forum, at a time of their choosing
(*MedImmune, Inc. v. Genentech, Inc.*, 549 U.S. 118 (2007)). It is uncommon at
this scale, but it is the reason the template says "will consider the remedies
available to it" rather than naming a suit, a court, and a date. Where the
recipient is a substantial commercial party with counsel, take advice before
sending.
